newsitem.title: USA: Morgan Stanley strategists see weak market in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley strategists see weak market in 1997.

text.p: Morgan Stanley Group Inc's top U.S. and global strategists are warning that next year will be the toughest that equities investors have faced since 1990, and may in fact represent the early stage of a bear market.

In a note outlining his view for the coming year, Morgan Stanley Global Strategist Barton Biggs wrote, "My intuition is that a correction at best and possibly a real bear market in equities has just begun, and that 1997 is going to be a down year for most U.S. equity portfolios."
"I think that in 1997 we will experience a true bear market in U.S. stocks ... with a decline of 20 percent to 30 percent peak to trough that will last six months," he said.

In an accompanying note, Byron Wien, the firm's U.S. strategist, said that right now "the market appears somewhat undervalued" based on a 6.5 percent long bond yield, but ultimately U.S. equities were due for a fall.

Wien and Biggs actually disagree on their reasons for a stock market decline next year -- Wien expects a rebound in the economy will push the yield on the U.S. long bond to between 7.5 and 8.0 percent but Biggs doubts such a scenario.
Instead, Biggs argues that U.S. stocks in particular have performed too well for too long, resulting in excessive valuations, though not to the degree experienced in Japan in the late 1980's.
Biggs, whose basic asset allocation adjustments were disclosed by the firm early this week, said he was "selling stocks around the world," principally in the U.S.

If the U.S. market does tail off, he argued, "it will bring down some of the other highfliers around the world with it, notably Hong Kong and Germany." Consequently, he cut exposure in Europe and Hong Kong.

Wien, who in April predicted a 1,000 point Dow decline but later withdrew that forecast, adhered to the view that stocks are eventually headed lower but argued such a decline is unlikely until after the first quarter of 1997.

Sometime after that, he said, "the effects of improving economic growth will be reflected in the financial markets" pushing up long term interest rates, a marked contrast to Biggs' view that the U.S. expansion is losing momentum and economies elsewhere are sluggish at best.
